units.summary: Groen states what the lectures set out to prove: that unbelief and revolution are bound together by nature and necessity. He explains why he publishes the manuscript almost unchanged. He then lists recent events and books that he says confirm his view, and ends with his two watchwords, Scripture and History.

parts.label: What the lectures try to prove
parts.covers: Groen says he gave these lectures in the winter of 1845-1846 to a few friends in his own study. They are an attempt to prove from history that unbelief and revolution are linked by nature and necessity. He argues that the direction now ruling constitutional law and learning, though not unopposed, came from rejecting the Gospel. It moves, he says, by lawful inference toward complete atheism and radicalism. He gives the manuscript almost unchanged.

units.summary: The introduction sets out the subject under four numbered heads: its choice, nature, use and plan. Groen argues that events since the rise of the revolution ideas flow from those ideas, and that the ideas flow from rejecting the Gospel. He tells his hearers what this study asks of them as Dutchmen and as Christians.

parts.label: The subject and why he chose it
parts.covers: Groen states the subject: since the revolution ideas arose, events have their cause in the natural growth of those ideas. He chose it after looking at what has happened in the Netherlands since 1795. He describes decline in trade, in political forms, in social order and in agreement about religion and law. Forms of government, circumstances and persons do not explain it, he argues; the cause lies in the ruling ideas.

parts.label: What he means by Revolution
parts.covers: Groen defines his terms. By Revolution he means not one change of rulers, nor only the storm in France, but the overturning of thought and attitude across Christendom. By revolution ideas he means liberty and equality, popular sovereignty, social contract and remaking society by agreement. He says the disasters of his fathers' time and his own flow from these ideas and from their source, rejection of the Gospel. Strict application, he argues, leads to absurdities and atrocities. Moderation that keeps the principle ends in wavering and arbitrary rule, and he counts the doctrinaires, the juste-milieu and the conservatives here. He argues that only the anti-revolutionary ground, where right rests on God's law, allows a real fight.

parts.covers: Groen sets out his plan and states his thesis: the age of revolution is the fruit of the revolution ideas. The first part of his argument is negative. He says the whole argument is historical, and that ideas and principles are facts of the highest rank. units.summary: Groen calls witnesses to show that careful learning in every age speaks against the constitutional law of the revolution. He appeals to the Bible, to history, to the ancients and to later political writers, above all Pitt, Burke, von Gentz, von Haller and Bilderdijk. He ends by claiming independence from every teacher but one.

parts.label: Not alone: appeal to earlier ages
parts.covers: Groen says most of his countrymen do not share his principles, which sometimes brings a feeling of isolation. He wants to show that he has allies and that thoughtful learning in all ages testifies against the revolution's constitutional law. He cites a saying of Luther on being sure of God's Word against the whole world. He also warns Christians against a masterful tone and against confusing their own reasoning with God's word.

parts.label: The Bible and the Reformers
parts.covers: Groen calls the Bible the book of books in the anti-revolutionary library. He does not look in it for an encyclopedia, as he says some have done. But he claims Holy Scripture shows the grounds of right and morality, authority and freedom, for nations and governments too. 'It is written' is the axe that cuts every root of revolutionary growth. He takes the Reformers as an example. Many a page of Luther and Calvyn, he says, shows they learned from God's commands about the authority of rulers.

parts.label: History against the revolution
parts.covers: Groen says the revolutionary theories are aimed against History as well as Revelation. They did appeal to history, he grants, and seemingly with reason. But shallow treatment let men read their own ideas into other peoples and times. He says this is no longer so in his day, at least not without strong contradiction. Newly known sources show, he says, that world history refutes the revolutionary teachings. He names Guizot among men who helped drive out the false analogies, though unwilling to admit those teachings are worthless.

parts.label: The Greek and Latin ancients
parts.covers: Groen appeals to the writings of the ancients. He grants that heathen wisdom was too often praised at the cost of Christian truth, but its bright side must be seen too. One-sided study of antiquity did harm, he grants, but it was republican harm, not revolutionary.

parts.covers: Groen says he is no unconditional admirer of von Haller, who went over to the Roman church and later slandered the Reformation. units.summary: Groen argues that the Revolution did not come from faults in the principles of the old public law. He defends four of them against attack. They are respect for historic rights and the self-rule of estates and corporations. They are also the divine right of government and the union of Church and State. He ends by saying these principles are the lasting pillars of freedom, law and order.

parts.label: Opening: old public law in outline
parts.covers: Groen opens the negative half of his argument. He says the Revolution did not come from faults in the old public law: not in its principles, its forms of state, or its abuses. He then sketches the old view of the state. Sovereignty meant independent authority. The state was God's institution, not man's work. Each authority was limited to its own sphere of rights.

parts.covers: Groen lists four charges against the old principles and takes the first. The charge is that respect for historic rights ignored the general principles of law. He answers that historic rights grew slowly out of the principle of law, which stood above events and not below them. He says no right was born from wrong, though prescription could in time clean a possession of its first stain.

parts.label: Third objection: divine right, its caricature
parts.covers: Groen turns to the divine right of government, which he says is widely mocked as a medieval error. He will treat the doctrine under three heads: its caricature, its nature and its effects. This part gives the caricature. He admits history shows such abuses but denies that defending a doctrine means defending its corruptions. He says both rulers and subjects stand under a higher power, and that this is the best guarantee of duty on both sides.

parts.label: Divine right: what Scripture says
parts.covers: Groen finds the meaning of divine right in Scripture: all power is ordained by God. He says 'ordained' means willed and instituted by God, not merely allowed. He limits the text to lawful power, and refuses to read it as a duty to obey a murderer or a crowned robber. He grants that Nero ruled when Paul wrote, and that a Christian is not always called to judge whether a power is lawful. He adds that divine right belongs to every form of government, republics included.

parts.label: Power as God's servant; anointing; 'by God's grace'

parts.covers: Groen draws the results of the doctrine. The sovereign answers to God alone, and knows that he does answer to God. units.summary: Groen asks whether the old European forms of state were so bad that they caused the Revolution. He describes them as a tempered monarchy: a prince who owns the sovereignty, limited by the rights of the estates. He ranks this form above the Asian monarchies and the ancient republics, and concludes that reform, not revolution, was possible.

parts.label: Opening: were the forms of state at fault?
parts.covers: Groen recalls that European public law rested on historical growth, organic life and God's sovereignty. He asks whether the forms of government were so faulty that a revolution was needed to overturn them. He says many take this as settled. He holds that misunderstanding of the old forms did harm in 1789, in 1815 and later. He will sketch first the nature and then the value of the old forms.

parts.label: Tempered monarchy: what monarchy is
parts.covers: Groen states that the European state was a tempered monarchy. He says the Dutch Republic is an exception, and even it looked like a monarchy with an absent prince. He asks his hearers not to apply what he says of princely power to the state of his own day, which rests on another ground. He reduces all forms to two: monarchy and republic. The difference lies in who owns the supreme authority. A monarchy is the rule of one person who holds authority as his own and by inheritance; the prince owns the sovereignty, not the subjects.

parts.label: Absolute authority and 'L'Etat, c'est moi'
parts.covers: Groen calls this authority complete, or absolute, but bound by higher ordinances. He rejects both the despotic and the revolutionary sense of the word. He leaves open whether Lodewijk XIV used it and what he meant by it. He adds that he is no supporter of that king. He warns that false terms hide the nature of things, as when people spoke of 'the Supreme Being' instead of the living God.

parts.label: The assemblies of the estates
parts.covers: Groen says the assemblies of the estates should be rated neither too high nor too low. They were not a fixed part of the form of state but an extraordinary measure each time. He calls the assemblies a bulwark against a ruler's greed, not a lever to overturn the throne.

parts.label: What the ancients wished for
parts.covers: Groen says the thinkers of Greece and Rome looked for what later grew from the Christian and Germanic principle. The East lacked respect for right and freedom; the ancient republics lacked a firm single authority. Europe joined the two. He quotes Cicero, who prefers a form mixed from all three. Tacitus says such a form is easier to praise than to make, and could not last. Groen answers that it did last. He points to Great Britain, and says a throne built on popular sovereignty can only be held up by despotism. He ends with a saying of Bolingbroke that Burke approved. A bracketed note says Dutch history with the House of Orange gave the Dutch monarchy a republican spirit.

parts.covers: Groen concludes that faults in the European forms of state did not cause the Revolution. He says their main lines condemn every revolution: no overturning was needed, and reform would have been possible. He quotes Burke's reproach to the French, made after mention of 1688. Yet he holds that there too every wished-for improvement could have been had on the historic foundations. He says the Dutch too preferred a revolutionary state to a historic one.

units.summary: Groen asks whether abuses in the old states caused the Revolution. He argues that they were misdescribed, exaggerated and already easing, and that the Revolution did not start with the oppressed. He concludes that its root lies deeper than politics, in theory.

parts.covers: Groen asks whether abuses had so corrupted the old states that reform was impossible. He says the test of the abuses shows the opposite. He admits the sins of earlier generations, but argues that the usual picture is often false. He says critics listed only the evil, piled up wrongs from a thousand years, and stirred up anger that was largely artificial.

He grants that the charge of tyranny against this king is partly true. He ends with a remark from a writer he does not name, which he calls very just. It says the new philosophy destroyed within a year what the most absolute king would hardly have dared touch.

He treats the first: constitutional law decayed when scholars, shaped by antiquity, came to see every state as an association of citizens. units.summary: Groen follows the same principle of unbelief into state law. Using long quotations from Rousseau's Contrat Social, he sets out a state built on contract and the people's will. He argues that it ends in total power over citizens, family, religion and property. He uses Montesquieu, the Illuminaten and Babeuf to show that, on revolutionary premises, the consistent extremists are right against the moderates.

parts.label: From sovereign reason to sovereign will
parts.covers: Groen says the same step leads from free thought to free action. Philosophy holds that man is good by nature, he says, so it puts the source of evil in the forms of society. Groen argues that without God's sovereignty nothing grounds authority, rank or duty. Then people are free and equal in the revolutionary sense. The state falls apart into isolated individuals, like the atoms in the system of Epicurus.

units.title_as_printed: DE REVOLUTIE-LEER IN STRIJD MET NATUUR EN REGT.
units.summary: Groen argues that the revolutionary theory collides with nature and law and so takes a fixed course. In religion it ends in indifference or idolatry. In politics it passes through five periods: preparation, development, reaction, renewed trial and resignation. He then says one thing stays the same throughout, the absolute power of the revolutionary state, and he brings five charges against it. Only a return to God's sovereignty can end it, he concludes.

parts.label: Opening: the theory meets resistance
parts.covers: Groen says the revolutionary theory cannot run freely. It fights nature, history, conscience and existing rights, and so it meets a reaction that bends its course. He asks what shape the applied doctrine of unbelief will take in real life. He announces a word on religion first, then a longer treatment of constitutional law.

parts.label: Unbelief in religion: indifference or idolatry
parts.covers: Groen traces what happens once faith in the living God declines and reason is held infallible. He says all revealed truth is driven out step by step. The human heart then either stops caring about truth at all, or flees into superstition and invented gods. He names mysticism, pantheism and Saint-Simonism as examples, and says only God can rescue.

units.summary: Groen states his thesis: the history of the last sixty years was the fruit of systematic unbelief. He sets out seven general features of the Revolution. He then begins the historical survey with the first period, Preparation, up to 1789. He argues that nearly all Europe, led by its princes, had taken up the new philosophy. In France, he says, the Revolution was inevitable long before 1789. The events of that year, he says, only proclaimed what was already done in people's minds.

units.summary: Groen treats the years 1789 to 1794 as the Revolution's period of development. He rejects the view that the king, the nobles and clergy, or the foreign powers drove a sound Revolution off course. He argues that each step, from the sovereign assembly to the fall of the Girondins, applied the doctrine more strictly. Principles, not men's wishes, carried France to 1793.

parts.label: Opening: the claim Groen will refute
parts.covers: Groen opens the second period, 1789 to 1794. He says its events match what he derived from the revolutionary principle itself. Many still argue that the Revolution was sound in 1789 and went wrong through accidents and resistance. He sets out two points to prove. First, the accidents were largely results of the doctrine themselves, and had less influence than people say. Second, the horrors were the false philosophy applied further. A long note takes St. Marc-Girardin's essay on Mirabeau as the example of this view and answers it from the Mirabeau-La Marck correspondence.

units.summary: Groen argues that the Terror was not an exception but the furthest working-out of the revolutionary principle. He studies Danton, Marat, St. Just and above all Robespierre, and finds their strength in sincere belief in the theory. He presents Robespierre as Rousseau's pupil, and closes by naming unbelief, the falling away from Christ, as the cause of the Revolution.

units.summary: Groen surveys France from the fall of Robespierre to his own day in three stages. These are the reaction that peaked under Napoleon, the Restoration of 1815 to 1830, and the July government after 1830. He argues that one thread of revolutionary ideas ties them together. Each regime that keeps the principle but fights its results must fall back on force. He closes by saying freedom will not come without giving up the revolutionary principle and returning to the Gospel.

Under point 1 he says the moderates who took power after the Terror kept the revolutionary theory. They drew their middle line by mere choice. He says such a government was strong through circumstances but weak for lack of principle, so it had to lean on force.

units.summary: Groen closes the lectures with four topics. They are the law of nations, the signs of the times, the Netherlands in the age of revolution, and the calling of Christians. He argues that the Revolution has shaped diplomacy and Dutch politics alike, and that liberalism cannot cure what its own principle causes. He ends by restating his thesis that the Revolution comes from the rejection of the Gospel, and by calling his hearers to faithful witness.

parts.label: Plan; theory of revolutionary international law
parts.covers: Groen opens the closing lecture with four topics. They are the law of nations, the signs of the times, the fatherland in the age of revolution, and personal calling and duty. He argues that the new law of nations rests on the same principles as revolutionary constitutional law. On this theory, he says, the 'sovereignty of mankind' leaves no treaty or acquired right safe against the general will. In practice, he claims, the will of all becomes the will of those with the stronger army.

But he argues that a change of forms leaves the root untouched. The same despotism of the revolutionary state, subjection of church to state and centralisation would remain. He says they can promise freedom but not give it, and that the sense of justice is growing dull.
